Meta — one of the largest and spendiest companies in the artificial intelligence trade — is slated to report earnings today after the bell. The report comes at a time when investors are increasingly worried about the amount of debt companies are taking on to fuel their AI ambitions. Specifically, investors are worried that companies like Meta took on a dangerous amount of debt to create products that have not yet proven that they will generate enough revenue to pay that money back. Meta’s message to investors will likely be something along the lines of: “trust the process.” Meta up until recently had little to show for its AI spend, and is expected to report $41.1 billion in capital expenditures for the quarter and $9.4 billion negative free cash flows, which would mark its first cash flow negative quarter since 2012. While we're on the topic, here’s what else the Street is expecting: Revenue at $63.3 million, up 23% year over year. Adjusted earnings per share at $6.79, down 6.3% year over year. Meta unveiled Muse, its personal AI agent, on Sept 8, meaning we’ll get a peak at how the new product performed in the first few weeks. The app surpassed 5 million downloads in its first three weeks, according to Sensor Tower data cited by multiple outlets .Wall Street appeared hopeful, sending Meta rallying in the weeks after the launch. Muse, which has a furry mascot that’s equal parts cute and unsettling, is one of the first big consumer AI products. You give it the keys to your email and credit cards and it can do things that are the bane of our existence, like make dinner reservations or order more Tide Pods. That’s a bit of a different play than its peers, which have made big bets on AI as a tool for corporations eager to do more with less humans. The relationship between AI companies and corporations is starting to show cracks but its relationship with consumers over a subscription based service is still in its early innings. It’s ultimately unclear if Muse will be the cashcow it needs to be in order to justify the amount Meta has spent on AI. The economics of a subscription product is also very different to Meta’s lucrative advertising business. And, as my colleague Walter Hickey pointed out earlier, it takes AI competitors like Amazon being willing to play ball in order for this thing to work as advertised. As we wade into a big week for tech earnings, the questions on everybody’s mind is as follows: How much more money are you going to spend and or borrow? When is the thing you’re working on going to make money? In Meta’s case, it has a shiny new product to talk about which is a better position than most of its peers. While it very well may report positive early adoption data, it still has to prove the product will be worth the many billions of dollars spent on it. title: 🥤 Soda streaming wars
body_text: Who’s for a game of six degrees of sartorial separation? Kevin Bacon, whose name lends itself to a game where people have to connect Hollywood figures back to the “Footloose” star in as few steps as possible, now hopes to be linked up with something much dearer to him: a box of clothes from the ‘90s. In a video posted to Instagram, the 68-year-old actor detailed the worldwide journey that the clothes have been on via New York, Memphis, France, Germany, Israel, and England, seemingly calling out FedEx as the offending courier behind the weeks-long route. Bacon sent out the plea with hopes to be reunited with the “old boots, old jeans, and old hats” in his original intended delivery destination of Ireland, and a spokesperson from the delivery giant has since confirmed they are now in direct contact with Bacon’s team. When you imagine the prolonged talks and tense negotiations that are thrashed out between some of the biggest names in global business, you might not imagine rooms of execs and franchisees sipping samples of innovative new tinctures, but that’s apparently how it went down in Texas over a couple of days in June , as KFC prepared to decide on a drink supplier moving forward. The choice, as it has often been for companies and customers alike through the years, was simple: Coke or Pepsi ? Follow in the footsteps of McDonald’s, Burger King, Wendy’s and many more by partnering with the most recognizable beverage brand of all time, or stick with Pepsi, the company that spun the chicken chain off as part of Yum! Brands in 1997 and has provided its drinks selection since the original acquisition some 40 years ago? This time, the Yum! fast-food behemoth went for Coca-Cola, switching from Pepsi in a move that mirrors the American soda-loving population at large. According to figures shared with Snacks by industry insights and analysis company Beverage Digest, Pepsi’s share of the carbonated soft drink market in the US has fallen from just over 13.6% at the start of the twenty-first century, to a little over 8% as of last year. In that time, Coca-Cola’s share has slipped much more slightly, down from 20.2% in 2000, to a still-strong 18.5% in 2025. In addition, last year was the third in a row where Dr. Pepper has taken a bigger share of the market than Pepsi, with Sprite and Diet Coke now also not far behind, taking 7.9% and 8% of soda case sales in the US, respectively. While it’s not the end of the world for Pepsi — the drinks giant will maintain its partnerships with international branches of KFC — it’s still a big blow, as Coca-Cola extends its already dominant position in the soft-drink fountain game, where it currently accounts for 70% of sales by volume, per separate Beverage Digest data . title: ❓Two Musk companies, one big question
body_text: Dyson wants to replicate the success of its vacuums and hair products but in your mouth. So far it is not going so well. The company’s $500 Camerajet toothbrush (powered by AI, of course) sprayed water across the bathroom and then stopped working, according to one Bloomberg reporter who tested the product . It was also incredibly hard to find stocked in any major retailer, they reported. Stocks ended a rocky week down on Friday. Elon Musk has found another way for his two companies to collaborate, leaving some wondering whether a more formal union could be next. On Thursday, CEO Elon Musk unveiled the long-awaited second-generation Tesla Roadster, a sports car developed with the help of his rocket company SpaceX . During a demonstration in Texas, the vehicle drove upside down, flipped through the air, and jumped over a row of other Teslas using rocket-style thrusters powered by compressed air. The company says the Roadster can accelerate from zero to 60 mph in less than a second, reach speeds exceeding 230 mph, and travel more than 300 miles on a single charge. “You’re going to see some crazy stuff tonight,” said Musk, who is CEO of both companies. “You’re going to see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company.” Deliveries for the long-delayed vehicle aren't expected until 2028. (The second gen Roadster was first announced by Musk in 2017 with delivery slated for 2020. Tesla's reservation agreement explicitly says the company cannot guarantee when the Roadster will be delivered or whether it will be delivered at all.) Musk also said he was "not sure it's necessarily legal in all jurisdictions." It will almost certainly spark some sort of regulatory review from the Federal Aviation Administration, Wired points out . But the Roadster's biggest significance may have less to do with its ability to fly than with the company helping it get off the ground. The unveiling has added fuel to speculation that Musk could eventually combine Tesla and SpaceX, bringing his electric-car business and rocket company under one roof. Prediction market traders increased the odds of a merger being announced by early next year. One Barclays analyst predicted that such a merger could happen before the end of this year. The Roadster is unlikely to do much for Tesla's bottom line. Musk has previously described the Roadster as a "small potato situation" that would not "move the needle in a major way financially." Tesla reports earnings this week, with analysts penciling in $19.6 billion in quarterly automotive sales, a 7.5% decline from the same period last year. As Tesla's traditional car business faces pressure, Musk is increasingly pitching investors on a future built around AI and robotics — areas where his companies' ambitions overlap. Veteran tech analyst Gene Munster put it best in an X post : “Two takeaways from tonight’s Roadster event. It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers. Elon can’t wait to bring $TSLA and $SPCX together.” The cumulative market capitalization for quantum computing companies IonQ , D-Wave , and Rigetti is virtually unchanged from where it was in early September 2025, right before those companies ramped in part on speculation over US government support. The fundamentals of the industry at large really haven’t meaningfully improved over the past year, nor have they deteriorated. And quantum computing is not a space where most traders were looking for hockey-stick growth now, it’s more about the prospect for technological breakthroughs that have the potential to spur parabolic operational improvements further down the road. The key underlying factor may be that the speculative energy just is not there anymore for this part of the market. Major pure-play quantum computing companies that have been around for a few years (like IonQ, D-Wave, and Rigetti) have seen call volumes drop precipitously from their 2025 peaks.
